individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper proposes LEAP, a learnable local structural positional encoding for graphs based on the differentiable Euler Characteristic Transform (DECT) and its local variant (ℓ-ECT). LEAP computes the ECT on normalized m-hop neighborhoods, then applies one of several learnable projections (linear, 1D convolution, DeepSets, transformer, or transformer with direction conditioning) to obtain a node embedding. It is designed to be end-to-end trainable and integrates with any GNN or transformer-style architecture. Experiments cover a synthetic graph classification task, multiple TU datasets (Letter, Fingerprint, COX2, BZR, DHFR, Alchemy, HIV), and ablations on projection strategy, neighborhood size, embedding dimension, and DECT hyperparameters. The paper reports consistent improvements over RWPE and LaPE across most settings.
Strengths: Novel combination of local ECTs with learnable projections, yielding an end-to-end trainable positional encoding that leverages both geometry and topology.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple datasets, architectures (GCN, GAT, NoMP), and PE baselines (RWPE, LaPE), with ablations on projection methods, locality, embedding dimension, and DECT hyperparameters.
The synthetic experiment demonstrates that LEAP can capture structural differences even when node features are uninformative, whereas standard MPNNs fail.
Introduction of the NoMP architecture provides a clean way to isolate the contribution of the PE by removing message passing.
The paper is well-structured and gives a clear explanation of the ECT, ℓ-ECT, and the proposed method, along with a discussion of limitations.
Reproducibility statement mentions code in supplementary materials, which supports reproducibility.
Weaknesses: The baseline comparison is limited to RWPE and LaPE; more recent or stronger PEs (e.g., SignNet, PEG, subgraph-based PEs) are not considered, weakening the claim of consistent superiority.
The synthetic dataset is extremely simple (graphs with 3 nodes, classify by edge count), so perfect accuracy may not strongly indicate general topological expressivity.
On the HIV dataset, LEAP does not outperform LaPE, and the paper only notes that it surpasses RWPE; this limits the generality of the claimed benefits.
Computational and memory costs of computing local ECTs for every node (with 16 directions and 16 thresholds) are not analyzed; scalability to large or dense graphs is unclear.

The theoretical guarantees of the exact ECT (e.g., injectivity) do not directly apply to the discretized, approximated, and normalized ECT used in LEAP, and the paper does not empirically investigate whether this affects expressivity.
The manuscript contains several formatting/typographical issues (e.g., corrupted equations, duplicated symbols, inconsistent notation) that can make it harder to follow.
The projection strategies are not compared against each other in the main results; the choice of projection appears dataset-dependent, yet the paper does not provide clear guidance on selecting one.
Questions: How does LEAP compare to more recent learnable PEs such as SignNet or PEG on standard benchmarks like ZINC or OGB?
What is the time and memory complexity of LEAP for graphs with high average degree or large diameter, and how does it scale to larger datasets?
In the synthetic task, would GCN/GAT with increased capacity or more message-passing layers also achieve perfect accuracy, or is this a fundamental representational limitation?

Since the differentiable ECT is only an approximation, is there empirical evidence that the encoded features preserve the theoretical expressivity of the exact ℓ-ECT? Could the approximation degrade performance on tasks requiring fine-grained structural distinctions?

How sensitive is LEAP to the choice of node features when they are high-dimensional or categorical? The HIV experiment uses a learned embedding; are there cases where LEAP underperforms because of the feature-dependence of the ECT?

The paper suggests that larger neighborhoods can hurt performance; is this due to the normalization or to the ECT approximation, and what are the implications for choosing the locality hyperparameter?
Limitations: LEAP is not a purely structural PE; it depends on node features (though these can be learned), which may be unavailable or noisy in some applications.
The method relies on a differentiable approximation of a discretized ECT, so theoretical guarantees of the exact ECT (e.g., injectivity) are not guaranteed to hold.

The number of hyperparameters (directions, thresholds, smoothing parameter, neighborhood hops, projection choice) is larger than that of RWPE or LaPE, and the paper does not provide a systematic guideline for tuning them.

The empirical evaluation is restricted to relatively small TU datasets and a synthetic task; performance on large-scale graphs (e.g., OGB) or on tasks requiring long-range dependencies is not demonstrated.
The paper does not analyze failure cases or situations where LEAP might underperform, beyond noting the HIV result and the drop with larger neighborhoods.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper introduces LEAP, a learnable local structural positional encoding for graphs based on a differentiable approximation of the local Euler Characteristic Transform (l-ECT). LEAP computes ECTs on local neighborhoods, normalizes features, and applies learnable projections (linear, 1D convolution, DeepSets, transformer, etc.) to produce node embeddings. It is end-to-end trainable and supports learning the direction vectors. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets (TUDataset, Alchemy, HIV) show consistent improvements over RWPE and LaPE across GCN, GAT, and a transformer without message passing (NoMP). Ablation studies examine neighborhood size, embedding dimension, projection strategies, and hyperparameter sensitivity.
Strengths: Novel integration of the local Euler Characteristic Transform into a learnable positional encoding, extending prior static l-ECT work to end-to-end training.
Comprehensive experiments across multiple datasets and architectures, with ablations on key hyperparameters (locality, embedding dimension, projection method).
The synthetic experiment demonstrates the ability to capture structural information independent of node features, albeit on a simple task.
Clear background and related work on ECT, PEs, and MPNN limitations.
The method is flexible and can be combined with various GNN architectures.
Weaknesses: The synthetic task is trivial (graphs with 3 nodes, edge counting) and the results do not convincingly demonstrate topological understanding beyond simple degree/edge information.
Baselines are limited to RWPE and LaPE; no comparison with more recent or stronger PEs (e.g., SignNet, PEG, or other learnable PEs), and hyperparameters for baselines may not be tuned.
No statistical significance tests are provided; many accuracy values have overlapping confidence intervals.
Computational complexity and scalability are not addressed; computing m-hop subgraphs and ECT for every node may be prohibitive on large graphs.
The paper proposes five projection strategies but provides no clear guidance on which to choose; results show no consistent winner, leaving practitioners without a principled selection method.
The claim of outperforming DECT is weakened by the fact that LEAP is used as a PE with additional backbone parameters, while DECT is used as a standalone classifier.
On the HIV dataset, LEAP does not outperform LaPE, highlighting that global information can be more important; this limitation is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed.
Questions: How does LEAP scale to graphs with millions of nodes? What is the time and memory complexity per node?
What is the theoretical justification for using the differentiable approximation (DECT) and normalization in terms of preserving the structural information of the exact ECT?
Are the performance improvements statistically significant? Were multiple seeds and significance tests (e.g., paired t-tests) considered?
Why does the 1-hop neighborhood consistently outperform larger hops? Could this be due to oversmoothing of local information?
Can LEAP be combined with global PEs (e.g., LaPE) to capture both local and global structure, and would this improve results on datasets like HIV?
How sensitive is LEAP to the quality of node features? What happens if features are noisy or missing?
Limitations: The method depends on node features; if features are uninformative or noisy, the ECT may not capture pure graph structure.
The differentiable approximation of the ECT and the normalization of features may break the theoretical guarantees (e.g., injectivity) of the exact ECT.
The computational and memory overhead of computing local subgraphs and ECTs for all nodes is not analyzed, potentially limiting scalability.
The paper does not provide a thorough comparison with recent state-of-the-art PEs or graph transformers, making it hard to assess the real-world advantage.
The choice of projection strategy is left as a hyperparameter with no clear recommendation, and the paper reports that no single strategy dominates.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper proposes LEAP, a learnable local structural positional encoding for graphs based on the local Euler Characteristic Transform (ℓ-ECT). It combines the differentiable ECT (DECT) with local neighborhoods to create node-level embeddings that are end-to-end trainable. The authors introduce five projection strategies, including permutation-invariant ones, and evaluate the method on synthetic and real-world datasets with GCN, GAT, and a transformer-based NoMP backbone. Results show that LEAP often outperforms RWPE and LaPE, and ablations explore the effects of locality, embedding dimension, and projection choice.
Strengths: Novel integration of the local Euler Characteristic Transform into deep learning as an end-to-end trainable positional encoding; the first to make ℓ-ECT learnable.
Extensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (TU benchmark, Alchemy, HIV) and architectures, demonstrating consistent improvements over RWPE and LaPE in many settings.
A synthetic task shows LEAP can capture structural information independent of node features, addressing a known limitation of MPNNs.
Five projection strategies are proposed, including permutation-invariant ones, providing flexibility and ensuring invariance to direction order.
Ablation studies analyze the impact of neighborhood size, PE dimension, and DECT hyperparameters, showing robustness to choices.
Weaknesses: The synthetic dataset is extremely simple (3-node graphs, classify by edge count), and the reason for perfect accuracy with random node features is not fully explained; it may not convincingly demonstrate ability to capture complex topological features.
No statistical significance tests (e.g., t-tests, confidence intervals) are reported; improvements over baselines are often small and may not be reliable.
The differentiable approximation of the ECT is not specified precisely (e.g., exact sigmoid formula), hindering reproducibility.
LEAP is not purely structural since it depends on node features, and the theoretical guarantees of the exact ECT do not carry over to the approximation or to non-geometric graphs.
On the HIV dataset, LaPE outperforms LEAP, indicating that global positional information can be more important for some tasks, and LEAP's local-only nature is a limitation.
Questions: What is the exact mathematical form of the differentiable approximation of the indicator function used in DECT? How are thresholds and direction parameters treated during training?
What is the computational cost (time and memory) of computing LEAP, especially for large graphs? Are there optimizations for local subgraph extraction and ECT computation?
In the synthetic experiment, how exactly does LEAP achieve 100% accuracy when node features are random? Could you provide a theoretical or empirical explanation?
Since LEAP is computed on local subgraphs, does the choice of m-hop neighborhood significantly affect scalability to large graphs?
Were any hyperparameters of the baselines (RWPE, LaPE) tuned per dataset? How did you ensure fair comparison?
Limitations: LEAP requires node features, so it cannot be applied to graphs without features without a learnable embedding layer.
The method introduces several hyperparameters (number of directions, thresholds, smoothing parameter) that require tuning, though the paper shows robustness.
The theoretical injectivity of the exact ECT does not hold for the approximated DECT or for non-geometric graphs, so expressivity is not guaranteed.
The local neighborhood size m is fixed in most experiments; the paper shows 1-hop is best, but this may not generalize to other tasks.
No negative societal impacts were identified, and no specific ethical concerns arise from this method.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: This paper proposes LEAP, a learnable local structural positional encoding for graphs based on the local Euler Characteristic Transform (l-ECT). The encoding computes differentiable ECTs on m-hop neighborhoods across multiple directions and thresholds, then projects the resulting matrix to a low-dimensional vector via learnable projection strategies (linear, 1D conv, DeepSets, transformer, transformer with direction information). The authors evaluate LEAP on synthetic and real-world graph classification datasets using GCN, GAT, and a transformer-based NoMP architecture, comparing against RWPE and LaPE. They report improved accuracy in most settings, with ablations on projection methods, neighborhood size, embedding dimension, and DECT hyperparameters.
Strengths: Novel integration of the local Euler Characteristic Transform as a learnable, end-to-end positional encoding for graphs, combining geometric and topological information.
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple architectures (GCN, GAT, NoMP) and datasets, with consistent improvements over RWPE and LaPE in most settings.
Ablation studies on projection strategies, locality (hop size), embedding dimensions, and DECT hyperparameters provide useful insights into design choices.
Synthetic experiment demonstrates LEAP's ability to capture structural information independent of node features, where standard GNNs fail.
The paper is well-structured and clearly presents the methodology, including five different projection strategies.
Weaknesses: Comparison is limited to RWPE and LaPE; many recent positional/structural encodings (e.g., PEG, SignNet, subgraph-based PEs) are not included, making the claimed superiority less robust.
No statistical significance testing is provided; some gains over baselines are small and may not be meaningful.

Computational complexity of LEAP is not analyzed; computing ECTs for each node's neighborhood across many directions and thresholds could be expensive for large or high-degree graphs, and scalability is not demonstrated.

The theoretical motivation (the connection between l-ECT and message passing) is not strongly tied to the empirical results, and the paper does not rigorously explain why LEAP works beyond empirical observation.
The synthetic task is trivial (graphs with only 3 nodes), which may not reflect the complexity of real-world structural differences.
Questions: What is the computational complexity of LEAP per node, and how does it scale to graphs with high degree or large diameter?
Why does learning directions sometimes degrade performance (e.g., GAT on Letter-M)? Is this due to overfitting or other factors?
Could the performance gains be attributed to the increased capacity from the learnable projection rather than the ECT itself? Have you compared with a random feature map of similar capacity?
How does LEAP compare with other recent local structural encodings, such as subgraph-based PEs or shortest-path distances?
In the HIV dataset, LaPE outperforms LEAP; what kind of global information is missing in LEAP, and could a combination with a global PE be beneficial?
Limitations: LEAP is not a purely structural PE; it requires node features to compute ECTs, although features can be learned.
The theoretical guarantees of ECT injectivity may not carry over to the differentiable approximation applied to non-geometric subgraphs.
LEAP introduces several hyperparameters (smoothing parameter, number of directions, thresholds, projection choice) that may require tuning, though the paper shows robustness.
The paper only evaluates on small-scale TU datasets; scalability to large graphs is not addressed.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_5

review.Summary: The paper introduces LEAP, a learnable local structural positional encoding for graphs based on the local Euler Characteristic Transform (ℓ-ECT). It combines the differentiable approximation of the ECT (DECT) with local neighborhoods, enabling end-to-end training, and presents five projection strategies to map the ECT matrix to a low-dimensional embedding. The method is evaluated on a synthetic edge-counting task and multiple TU benchmark datasets, with ablations on locality, embedding dimension, projection strategy, and DECT hyperparameters. Results indicate that LEAP often improves accuracy over no PE, RWPE, and LaPE when combined with GCN, GAT, or a transformer-like NoMP backbone, especially when the sampling directions are learned.
Strengths: The idea of a learnable, local ECT-based positional encoding is novel and timely, drawing on theoretical expressivity results of ECTs.
The method is flexible: it supports end-to-end training, learnable directions, multiple projection strategies (including permutation-invariant ones), and can be plugged into various backbones.
The synthetic experiment demonstrates that LEAP can capture edge-count structure even when node features are uninformative, while standard GCN/GAT fail.
The paper provides extensive ablations on projection strategy, embedding dimension, locality, and DECT hyperparameters, showing robustness to these choices.
The writing is generally clear and the reproducibility statement indicates that code will be provided.
Weaknesses: The synthetic dataset is extremely simple (graphs with 3 nodes classified by edge count) and does not convincingly demonstrate the claimed ability to capture complex topological features; harder substructure-counting tasks are not evaluated.

Baselines are limited to RWPE and LaPE; more recent and stronger positional/structural encodings (e.g., SignNet, SPE, persistent-homology-based PEs) are not compared, despite being cited in the related work.
The paper does not clearly specify how node features are obtained for datasets that may lack natural node attributes (e.g., Letter datasets), which is critical for reproducing the method.
Claims of consistent improvement are weakened by modest and often statistically overlapping results on small-molecule datasets, and the HIV experiment shows LaPE outperforming LEAP.
No computational complexity analysis is provided; per-node computation of ECTs on m-hop subgraphs with a 16x16 grid may become prohibitive for large graphs or node-level tasks.
The paper does not report multiple seeds or statistical significance tests; the statement of a 'fixed seed' raises concerns about the reliability of the reported mean±std values.
Questions: How are node features defined for datasets like Letter-H/M/L and Fingerprint that may not have natural node attributes? Are constant or learned features used, and how does this affect the ECT computation?

How many independent runs were performed? Are the reported means and standard deviations computed over 5-fold cross-validation only, and were differences between methods tested for statistical significance?
What is the exact formulation of the differentiable ECT approximation (e.g., sigmoid temperature, threshold grid), and how is the gradient learned with respect to the directions?
How does LEAP scale to large graphs (e.g., a single graph with millions of nodes) where per-node m-hop subgraph ECT computation may be computationally expensive?
Could LEAP be combined with other PEs to provide complementary information, and does it capture structure that is orthogonal to RWPE and LaPE?
What happens when all node features in a neighborhood are identical after centering (i.e., maximum norm is zero)? Is there a degeneracy in the normalization step?
Limitations: LEAP is not a purely structural PE: it depends on node features, and its theoretical guarantees (e.g., injectivity) do not directly apply to arbitrary discrete graphs since normalized neighborhoods are not necessarily geometric.
The method introduces additional hyperparameters (number of directions, number of thresholds, smoothing parameter, locality radius) that require tuning, although ablations suggest robustness.
The empirical evaluation is limited to relatively small/mid-sized TUDatasets; no large-scale node-level benchmarks are considered.

Two of the proposed projection strategies (linear and 1D convolution) are not permutation invariant with respect to the order of ECCs, which may limit their ability to encode direction-independent structure, though this is not analyzed.
The paper does not discuss potential negative societal impacts, but they are likely minimal for this type of methodological work.

review.Summary: The paper introduces LEAP, a learnable local structural positional encoding for graphs based on the local Euler Characteristic Transform (ℓ-ECT). LEAP computes differentiable ECTs on normalized m-hop neighborhoods across multiple directions and thresholds, then applies one of five learnable projection strategies (linear, 1D convolution, DeepSets, transformer, or transformer with direction conditioning) to produce node embeddings. The method is end-to-end trainable and can be integrated with GNNs or transformer-style architectures. Experiments on a synthetic edge-counting task, multiple TUDatasets, and Alchemy/HIV evaluate LEAP against RWPE and LaPE using GCN, GAT, and a transformer without message passing (NoMP). The paper reports consistent improvements over baselines in most settings, along with ablations on projection strategy, neighborhood size, embedding dimension, and DECT hyperparameters.
Strengths: Novel synthesis of the local Euler Characteristic Transform and modern deep learning, making the ℓ-ECT learnable for graph positional encodings.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple datasets, architectures, and baselines, including ablations on key components.
The synthetic experiment demonstrates that LEAP can capture structural information (e.g., edge counts) even when node features are uninformative, while standard MPNNs fail.
Flexible design: supports end-to-end training, learnable directions, multiple permutation-invariant projection strategies, and integration with various backbones.
Clear exposition of the methodology and related background on ECTs, PEs, and MPNN limitations.
Weaknesses: Baselines are limited to RWPE and LaPE; more recent and potentially stronger PEs (e.g., SignNet, PEG, subgraph-based PEs) are not compared, weakening the claim of consistent superiority.
No statistical significance tests (e.g., paired t-tests, confidence intervals) are reported; many improvements are small with overlapping variance.
Computational and memory complexity of per-node local ECT computation is not analyzed; scalability to large or dense graphs is unknown.
Theoretical guarantees of the exact ECT (e.g., injectivity) do not directly apply to the differentiable approximation and normalization used in LEAP, and the paper does not empirically probe this.
The synthetic task (3-node graphs by edge count) is trivially simple and does not convincingly demonstrate complex topological expressivity.
On HIV, LaPE outperforms LEAP, indicating that global information can be more important; LEAP's local-only nature is a limitation.
Five projection strategies are proposed, but no clear guidance is given on selection; results show dataset-dependent performance, leaving a practical gap.
The paper does not specify how node features are defined for datasets lacking natural attributes, which hinders reproducibility.
Questions: How does LEAP compare to stronger recent PEs like SignNet, PEG, or persistent-homology-based methods on standard benchmarks (e.g., ZINC, OGB)?
What is the time and memory complexity of LEAP per node? How does it scale to graphs with high degree or millions of nodes?
Are the reported improvements statistically significant? Were multiple seeds and paired significance tests performed?
What is the exact formulation of the differentiable approximation (e.g., sigmoid temperature, threshold grid) and how are directions learned?
How does LEAP behave when node features are noisy or categorical? Is the method still robust?
Why does the 1-hop neighborhood consistently perform best? Could this indicate that larger hops oversmooth or dilute structural information?
Could LEAP be combined with global PEs (e.g., LaPE) to capture both local and global structure, and would this improve results on HIV?
Limitations: LEAP is not purely structural; it depends on node features (though these can be learned), which may be unavailable or noisy in some applications.
The differentiable approximation of the ECT and the normalization of features break the theoretical guarantees of the exact ECT, so injectivity is not guaranteed.

The method introduces several hyperparameters (directions, thresholds, smoothing, locality radius, projection choice) that require tuning; ablation suggests robustness, but no systematic guideline is provided.
Scalability is unaddressed: computing ECTs for m-hop subgraphs with a 16×16 grid for every node may be prohibitive for large or dense graphs.
The empirical evaluation is confined to small/mid-sized TUDatasets and a synthetic toy; performance on large-scale graph-level or node-level tasks is not demonstrated.
The choice of projection strategy is left as a hyperparameter with no principled way to select, and some projections are not permutation-invariant to direction order.
